source_text: Χρόνος δὲ οὗτος πάντων γέμει τῶν ἐναντιωτήτων, τοκετῶν, εἶτα θανάτων, βλαστήσεως φυτῶν, εἶτα ἀνατροπῆς· ἰάσεων καὶ ἀναιρέσεων, οἴκων τε εὐορθώσεως καὶ καταλύσεως, κλαυθμῶν καὶ γελώτων, κοπετῶν καὶ ὀρχημάτων. Νῦν μὲν συνάγει τις τὰ ἀπὸ γῆς, νῦν δὲ ἐξέβαλε· καὶ ποτὲ μὲν ἐπιμέμηνε γυναικί, ποτὲ δὲ αὐτὴν ἀποστυχεῖ. Καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐζήτησέ τις ὁτιοῦν, νῦν δὲ ἀπώλεσε· καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐφύλαξε, νῦν δὲ προήκατο· ἄλλοτε ἀπέκτεινεν, ἄλλοτε ἐφονεύθη· ἐλάλησεν, εἶτα ἡσύχασεν· ἠγάπησεν, εἶτα ἐμίσησε. Τὰ γὰρ ἐν ἀνθρώποις πράγματα ποτὲ μὲν πολεμεῖται, ἄλλοτε δὲ εἰρηνεύεται, ὀξυρρόπως τῶν πραγμάτων ἐξ ἀγαθῶν εἶναι δοκούντων εἰς ὁμολογούμενα κακὰ μεταπιπτόντων. Παυσώμεθα τοίνυν ἐξ ἀνονήτων μόχθων. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἅπαντα, ὥς γέ μοι δοκεῖ, κέντροις ἰοβόλοις ἀνθρώπους ἐξοιστρεῖν ἐτέθη. Καιροσκόπος δή τις πονηρὸς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦτον περικέχηνεν, ἀφανίσαι ὑπερδιατεινόμενος τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ πλάσμα, ἐξ ἀρχῆς αὐτῷ μέχρι τέλους πολεμεῖν ᾑρημένος. Πέπεισμαι τοίνυν τὰ μέγιστα ἀγαθὰ ἀνθρώπῳ εὐθυμίαν καὶ εὐποιΐαν ὑπάρχειν, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ τὴν πρόσκαιρον ταύτην ἀπόλαυσιν ἐκ Θεοῦ παραγενέσθαι μόνον, εἰ δικαιοσύνη τῶν πράξεων ἡγοῖτο. Τῶν δὲ αἰωνίων καὶ ἀφθάρτων πραγμάτων, ὅσα ὁ Θεὸς παγίως ὥρισεν, οὔτε τι ἀφελεῖν, οὔτε τι προσθεῖναι δυνατόν. ᾯ τινι οὖν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν, ἐκεῖνα φοβερά τε ὁμοῦ καὶ θαυμαστά· καὶ τὰ μὲν γενόμενα, ἕστηκε· τὰ δὲ ἐσόμενα, ἤδη κατὰ τὸ προεγνῶσθαι γεγένηται. Θεῷ δὲ κέχρηται ὁ ἀδικούμενος βοηθῷ.
thought_title: A time for every opposite, and God's work stands fixed
orientation: Human affairs swing between opposites, while what God has fixed can be neither added to nor taken away.
pass_a_gloss: This time is full of all the oppositions: of childbirths, then of deaths; of sprouting of plants, then of overturning; of healings and of destructions, killings; of setting-upright of houses and of dissolution; of weepings and laughters; of mournings, beatings of the breast, and dances. Now someone gathers the things from the earth, now he threw them out; and at one time he is mad for a woman, at another he abhors her. And now someone sought anything whatever, now he lost it; and now he guarded, now he let go; at one time he killed, at another he was slain; he spoke, then he kept quiet; he loved, then he hated. For the affairs among men are at one time warred, at another made peaceful, the affairs falling over quickly-turning from things seeming to be good into acknowledged evils. Let us cease therefore from profitless toils. For all these things, as it seems to me, were placed to goad men to madness with poison-shooting stings. An evil watcher for the right moment gapes around this age, straining exceedingly to make vanish the molded creature of God, having chosen to war against it from beginning to end. I am persuaded therefore that the greatest goods for a human being are cheerfulness and well-doing, and indeed that this temporary enjoyment comes from God only if righteousness should lead the actions. But of the eternal and incorruptible affairs, as many as God fixed firmly, it is possible neither to remove anything nor to add anything. To whomever then (but it is), those things are fearful and wonderful together; and the things that have come to be stand; and the things that will be have already come to be according to being foreknown. And the one wronged has God as helper.

pass_b_english: This present time is full of every kind of opposite: births, then deaths; the sprouting of plants, then their uprooting (Ecclesiastes 3:1-2); healings and killings, the building of houses and their pulling down (Ecclesiastes 3:3); weeping and laughter, mourning and dancing (Ecclesiastes 3:4). Now someone gathers what comes from the earth, and now he has thrown it away; at one time he is mad with passion for a woman, at another he loathes her (Ecclesiastes 3:5). Now someone has sought something, and now he has lost it; now he has kept it, and now he has let it go (Ecclesiastes 3:6); at one time he killed, at another he was killed; he spoke, then fell silent (Ecclesiastes 3:7); he loved, then hated (Ecclesiastes 3:8). For human affairs are now at war and now at peace (Ecclesiastes 3:8), as things swing quickly from what seemed good into what all admit is evil.

Let us stop, then, our useless toils (Ecclesiastes 3:9). For all these things, it seems to me, were set there to drive human beings into frenzy with venomous stings (Ecclesiastes 3:10). A wicked one who watches for his chance gapes greedily over this age, straining with all his might to destroy what God has formed, for he has chosen to make war on it from beginning to end (Ecclesiastes 3:11).

I am convinced, then, that the greatest goods for a human being are good cheer and doing good (Ecclesiastes 3:12), and that even this passing enjoyment comes from God only if righteousness guides one's actions (Ecclesiastes 3:13). But from the eternal and incorruptible things that God has firmly fixed, nothing can be taken away and nothing added (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Yet to anyone at all, those things are at once fearful and wonderful. What has come to be stands fast, and what is still to be has already come to be, in that it is foreknown; and the one who suffers wrong has God for his helper (Ecclesiastes 3:15).
notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 3:1-15. Doubtful reading (flagged in the source row, same words in both prints): ᾯ τινι οὖν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν, ἐκεῖνα φοβερά τε ὁμοῦ καὶ θαυμαστά looks corrupt; 'To anyone at all' renders ᾯ τινι οὖν loosely, construed as the dative of ὁστισοῦν ('to anyone whatever'), and ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν ('but it is') is given as 'Yet ... those things are'. Reviewer checked the Opera omnia zoom (z106c, at C): it reads Ὧι τινι οὖν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν, as the copy-text. The Vossius Latin renders only 'Verum formidolosae simul et admirabiles illae sunt'. The sentence echoes Ecclesiastes 3:14b ('God has done it, so that people fear before Him') and is left uncited. 'What comes from the earth' (τὰ ἀπὸ γῆς) stands for the stones of 3:5; ἀποστυχεῖ is read as ἀποστυγεῖ ('loathes'). The tense shifts (present, then aorist) in the list of opposites are kept. 'A wicked one who watches for his chance' renders καιροσκόπος ... πονηρός; Gregory means the devil but does not name him, so neither does the English. 'What God has formed' renders τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ πλάσμα (the creature God molded; compare Genesis 2:7, not cited as uncertain). The citation of 3:11 rests on the LXX wording αἰῶνα and ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς καὶ μέχρι τέλους, which Gregory turns into the devil's war on God's work. 'Has God for his helper' answers 3:15b ('God seeks what has been driven away').
